sweep_summary: Two title-keyword items only. (1) Owens 1980 (BSOAS 43:277-287) is paywalled at Cambridge Core; only the Firthian-analysis extract is open and it says nothing about stress placement; no open copy found on archive.org or Cambridge; the two Essex theses count it as a descriptive account of Eastern Libyan syllabification/epenthesis rather than a stress statement; priority medium since the catalog already rests on Owens 1984 via Kager 2009. (2) Cangemi & D'Imperio 2011 is a HAL-indexed AISV paper on Neapolitan Italian sentence modality/timing — a Glottolog misfiling, irrelevant. Two open Essex PhD theses already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass were read in full for their stress chapters: Altubuly 2016 (Tripoli LA) gives a first-hand weight-sensitive rule (superheavy final > heavy penult > antepenult) with documented exceptions, confirming the catalog's 'weight' coding; Bobaker 2019 (Tobruq, Eastern LA) refines it with word-class-conditioned final-CVC stress (verbs/type-1 nouns final, type-2 nouns/adjectives initial) and stress-repelling dual suffixes, and warns that Tobruq differs from the Benghazi dialect usually taken as representative. Neither supersedes Kager 2009/Owens 1984 as the deciding source for the Cyrenaican variety, but both are better first-hand sources than a secondary restatement and should be added to the per-language bibliography.org queries and the theses' literature reviews instead of web searches.

new_statements.quote: LA stress has similar rules to standard Arabic: (1) stress the final superheavy syllable as in /ħi'saːb/ account. (2) if there is no superheavy syllable, then stress the heavy penultimate syllable /ka'tabna/ we wrote (3) if there is no heavy penultimate syllable, then stress the antepenultimate one as in 'rasama /he drew/. The three patterns mentioned above have equivalent patterns in LA: min'daːr /mattress/ with a superheavy stressed syllable, /gar'ʒuːma/ throat with a heavy penultimate syllable and /'mariga/ bib with a light antepenultimate one.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive stress within a three-syllable right-edge window: a superheavy (CVVC/CVCC) final syllable is stressed; otherwise a heavy penult; otherwise the antepenult, penult being the default position. First-hand, native-speaker description of Tripoli Libyan Arabic with a chapter-long treatment of the exceptions (final CVC with a low vowel in disyllables, epenthesis/syncope interactions, lexical and word-class-conditioned cases). Confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Confirms the class-level 'weight' coding (quantity-sensitive, bounded right three-syllable window, superheavy ultima > heavy penult > antepenult), but for the WESTERN (Tripoli) variety; the catalog's coded lect is the Cyrenaican Jebel Bedouin (Eastern Libyan) dialect via Kager 2009 restating Owens 1984 / Mitchell 1975, and Al Tubuly herself (fn. 5, p. 64) and Bobaker (2018, p. 124) say the eastern and western systems differ in detail (final-CVC weight, foot analysis). File Al Tubuly 2016 as a first-hand SUPPORTING source for the roster language, not as the deciding source for the coded lect.

tone_statements.quote: Afroasiatic languages have phonologized pitch into different prosodic systems that vary from a demarcative accent system, e.g. Berber; to a lexical stress system, e.g. Tripoli Arabic; a pitch accent system, e.g. Juba Arabic; and a tone system, e.g. Hausa and Zaar [...] 5.1 TRIPOLI ARABIC PROSODIC SYSTEM. Tripoli Arabic has a lexical stress system, i.e. every content word is stressed on one of its syllables. The place of the stress is not fixed but it is predictable (Pereira 2010: 88-89). The prosodic structure of Tripoli Arabic also involves sentence-level prominence stress: within a sentence, some words are more prominent than others and stress thus concerns one particular syllable which is perceived as the most prominent in the sentence.

sources.quote: (37) TLA stress algorithm (a) Stress the right most heavy syllable CVV or CVVC of a monomorphemic word or plural suffix. /mos.ta.ˈtˤi:l/ 'rectangular' /ba.ˈtˤa:.tˤa/ 'potato' (b) Otherwise stress the penultimate CVV or CVVC of a plural suffix, or lengthen the V-final inflectional suffix that precedes an object suffix. (38) (a) Stress the left-most light CV if the syllable pattern is a CV.CVC noun (type 2) and CV.CVC adjective. /ˈʕa.lam/ 'flag' /ˈha.bal/ 'idiot' (b) Heavy ultimate CVVC is not stressed if it is a dual suffix. /ˈmas.ra.fe:n/ 'two banks' (pp. 146-147)
sources.note: First-hand account of Tobruq (Eastern Libyan) Arabic: stress is quantity-sensitive for long-vowel syllables (rightmost CVV/CVVC), but final CVC weight is word-class conditioned — CV.CVC verbs and 'type 1' nouns take final stress, 'type 2' nouns and all CV.CVC adjectives take initial stress — so stress is contrastive within the lexicon (/ʕa.ˈraf/ 'knew' vs /ˈʕa.raf/ 'custom', p. 125-126); the dual suffix -e:n repels stress; final-syllable extrametricality when the final is light (§5.2.7.2). sources.locator: Introduction and section 5.1 'Tripoli Arabic prosodic system'; published chapter pp. 63-115
sources.note: Classifies Tripoli Arabic as a lexical stress system (predictable, non-fixed word stress, after Pereira 2010: 88-89) in explicit contrast to the pitch accent system of Juba Arabic and the tone systems of Zaar/Hausa; pitch is used only post-lexically (declination in assertions/wh-questions, penultimate rise in yes/no questions, topic contour with final lengthening + pause + reset, focus by expanded pitch range). No lexical tone.
